about.title: Commerce Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Commerce residents rely on a mix of local clinics and larger Los Angeles County hospital systems for care, and most visits end the way they're supposed to. But when a provider misses a diagnosis, makes a surgical error, or mismanages medication, the harm can follow a patient for years. California's MICRA law puts strict boundaries around these cases — short notice periods, a required 90-day pre-suit warning to the provider, and a mandatory qualified medical expert to establish that the standard of care was broken. A bad result by itself doesn't mean malpractice happened; the law requires proof that a provider fell below the accepted standard of care and that this failure caused real harm. If you believe a hospital, clinic, or physician serving the Commerce area made an error that hurt you, LawProactive can connect you with an independent attorney, free of charge, to review what happened.

items.title: Deadlines Move Fast Under MICRA
items.desc: California generally gives you one year from discovering the harm, and never more than three years from the injury itself, to act. Missing the 90-day pre-suit notice window can also delay or bar a claim, so early guidance matters.

items.title: Expert Proof Is Required, Not Optional
items.desc: California law almost always requires a qualified medical expert to show a provider's care fell below the accepted standard. An independent attorney can help arrange that kind of review before deadlines close in.

items.title: Understanding the Non-Economic Damages Cap
items.desc: MICRA sets a cap on non-economic damages that rises each year, and how a claim is built can affect what's recoverable. An attorney familiar with these rules can explain how the current cap applies to your situation.

items.question: I had a bad outcome after surgery near Commerce — does that mean it's malpractice?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California law requires proof that a provider's care fell below the accepted medical standard and that this failure caused your harm, not just that the result was disappointing. A qualified medical expert typically has to review the case to determine whether that standard was actually broken.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a claim in Commerce?
items.answer: Under MICRA, you generally have one year from when you discovered or reasonably should have discovered the harm, but never more than three years from the date of the injury. There's also a required 90-day notice you must send the provider before filing suit, so it's worth getting guidance sooner rather than later.

items.question: Are there limits on what I can recover for pain and suffering?
items.answer: Yes. MICRA places a cap on non-economic damages such as pain and suffering, though that cap is scheduled to rise each year. Economic damages like medical bills and lost income are handled separately and aren't subject to that same cap.

items.question: Does LawProactive charge anything to connect me with an attorney in Commerce?
items.answer: No. LawProactive is a free service, and attorneys in the network work on contingency, meaning there's no fee unless you recover compensation. We simply help connect you with an independent attorney who can evaluate your situation.
